title: Tencent's GTA Rival Last Sentinel Collapses After Six Years and Hundreds of Millions
excerpt: Lightspeed LA's ambitious open-world game, led by a Rockstar Games veteran, has been effectively abandoned after internal playtests bombed, resulting in 80 layoffs at the Irvine-based studio.
body:
• Tencent's Lightspeed LA studio spent six years and hundreds of millions of dollars building Last Sentinel, a cyberpunk open-world game pitched as a Grand Theft Auto competitor, only to effectively cancel it this week.
  • Internal playtests earlier this year reportedly failed to impress, with the game described as "janky" and far below the quality bar Tencent expected from a project designed to rival Rockstar Games.
  • Eighty developers have been laid off from the Irvine, California studio, though Lightspeed LA says it remains open and will continue making games.
  • The collapse follows a pattern of Chinese gaming giants retreating from expensive Western studio investments after discovering that building AAA console games from scratch is far harder than adapting mobile hits.

A Flagship Game That Never Showed Gameplay

Last Sentinel debuted with a glossy, cinematic trailer at The Game Awards in December 2023, promising an open-world action game set in a dystopian, near-future Tokyo. Developed by Lightspeed LA, a US subsidiary of Tencent's Lightspeed Studios, the project was led by Steve Martin, a 14-year Rockstar Games veteran who had worked on Grand Theft Auto V and Red Dead Redemption 2. The studio, based in Irvine, California, had hired experienced developers from The Last of Us, Jedi: Fallen Order, and Uncharted, and later brought on veteran voice actor Troy Baker as performance director.

https://x.com/Kotaku/status/2083253221670130103

Three years after that reveal, the game never once showed actual gameplay footage. According to a Bloomberg report by Jason Schreier, Tencent has decided not to move forward with the project following a devastating internal review, leading to the layoff of 80 employees on July 28.

"Tencent set out to take on Grand Theft Auto. After six years, hundreds of millions of dollars, and a whole lot of big promises, they 'rebooted' (most likely canceled) Last Sentinel this week and laid off 80 people."

— Jason Schreier, Bloomberg

Where It Went Wrong

The trouble, according to Bloomberg's reporting, ran deep. Behind-closed-doors playtests held earlier in 2026 drew negative reactions. Tencent's Chinese executives were reportedly unhappy with the game's progress. People who worked on the project told Bloomberg that Last Sentinel felt "janky" and did not hit the quality bar expected from a title pitched as Tencent's answer to Grand Theft Auto.

Bloomberg cited a lack of clear creative direction, vision, and strong management as core problems. The project was described as overly ambitious for a brand-new studio attempting to build a GTA-caliber cyberpunk open world with just a few hundred developers. Whatever the precise causes, the game blew through budgets and deadlines repeatedly.

A veteran Tencent designer was reportedly brought in to steer the project back on track. But when he and Martin addressed employees on July 28, the message was that Tencent was no longer moving forward with Last Sentinel as planned. A Lightspeed spokesperson told Bloomberg that the studio "remains open and continues to build games," suggesting some altered version of the project could survive. Insider Gaming, however, reported the consensus is that Last Sentinel is effectively dead.

A Pattern of Expensive Failures

The collapse of Last Sentinel is not an isolated incident. It fits squarely into a broader pattern of Chinese gaming giants pouring billions into Western AAA game development only to walk away empty-handed.

Tencent shut down TiMi Montreal earlier this year, five years after founding the studio with a mandate to build AAA open-world titles. TiMi Montreal, led by former Assassin's Creed franchise head Ashraf Ismail, never released a single game. In 2023, Tencent also closed Team Kaiju, another LA-based studio staffed with former Halo and Battlefield leads, before it shipped anything.

NetEase, China's other gaming giant, has similarly pulled funding from half a dozen North American studios over the past year. A February report from Niko Partners attributed the retreat partly to the success of China-developed games like Black Myth: Wukong and Genshin Impact, which demonstrated that studios based in China could produce globally competitive titles at a fraction of the cost of Western operations.

What It Means for the Industry

The retreat carries real consequences for the thousands of game developers working in the US, where the industry has been battered by relentless layoffs since 2023. More than 30,000 gaming jobs have been cut over the past three years. Tencent's decision to scale back its most ambitious Western project signals that one of the industry's deepest pockets is no longer willing to bankroll the kind of enormous, risky bets that AAA console development demands.

For aspiring game developers in the Indian diaspora and beyond, the lesson is stark. Even with hundreds of millions of dollars, a team of industry veterans, and one of the world's largest gaming companies backing the project, building a game to rival Grand Theft Auto proved to be an impossible task. With GTA VI looming over the industry ahead of its planned November 2026 launch, few companies appear willing to compete head-on with Rockstar Games anymore.
nri_angle: Tencent's pullback from Western AAA gaming signals a broader retreat by Chinese tech giants from costly overseas studios, a shift that could affect South Asian gaming professionals in the US industry already reeling from mass layoffs.
